parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a carpenter to order a made-to-measure bookcase.
script: Good afternoon, Tidewell Joinery, Dylan speaking.
Oh, hello. I saw your advert on the noticeboard at the library, and I'm hoping you can make a bookcase for me. Something made to measure.
Yes, that's exactly what we do. I'll fill in an enquiry form while we talk, if that's all right. Could I have your name?
Sorry, how do you spell the surname?
Wexcombe, lovely. And what's the best number to reach you on?
No, 462. The last three digits are 4, 6, 2.
Got it, thanks. So, what did you have in mind?
It's for the sitting room, along the wall beside the fireplace. At the moment I've got some old shelves that are falling to bits.
Right. Are you thinking of pine? It's the cheapest option we offer.
I did think so at first, but pine marks so easily, and I've got a cat. I'd rather have oak, even if it costs more. My brother has an oak table that's lasted for twenty years.
Oak's a good choice. We buy it from a sawmill near here, so it's reasonably priced. Now, the measurements. How tall do you want it to be?
Well, the ceiling's 2 metres 40, but I'd like it to stop well short of that. I thought about 2 metres.
Hmm. Haven't you got a picture rail running round the room?
Oh, yes. I'd forgotten. It's at 2 metres 20.
Then I'd suggest leaving a gap of 10 centimetres below it, so it doesn't look cramped. That makes it 210 centimetres.

The wall is 2 metres 20 between the fireplace and the window. I was going to say 160 centimetres, but I've got so many books that I'd rather use more of the wall. If I leave 20 centimetres at each end, that gives me 180.
180 is a good width. Any wider and the shelves would start to sag in the middle. How many shelves do you want?
With 210 centimetres to play with, you could have six quite comfortably, and still leave room for tall art books at the bottom. They're adjustable, so you can move them later.
Anything else? A lot of people like a cupboard section at the bottom for games and paperwork.
Yes, two cupboards with doors. Not drawers. My last bookcase had drawers that kept sticking.
Two cupboards, no problem. Now, for the finish, we can do a natural oil, which looks very soft, or a varnish, either gloss or matt.
Not gloss. It's far too shiny for that room. A matt varnish, please.

Matt, fine. Now, delivery. We're booked up for about three weeks, but we do deliver and fit it ourselves. Our van is in for a service on Mondays, so I'd have to say no to Monday. Would Tuesday suit you?
I'm teaching all day on Tuesdays and Thursdays, I'm afraid. Wednesday would be fine, any time in the morning.
Wednesday morning, then. I'll put you down for that.

For oak, 180 by 210, with six shelves and two cupboards, I make it 680 pounds, and that includes the matt varnish. We ask for a deposit of a quarter of the price when you order, so that's 170 pounds. The remaining 510 pounds is paid when we deliver.
That's fine. Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone?
Of course. Let me just take a few more details and then I'll put you through to our office.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A volunteer organiser explains how a beach clean-up day will work.
script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for coming along to this briefing. For those who haven't met me, I'm Maddie Corrigan, and I'm coordinating Saturday's clean-up at Saltgrass Bay. Last year 140 people turned out and we collected over 2 tonnes of rubbish in a single morning, and this year we're hoping to beat that.

Let me start with the practical details. We'll be meeting outside the lifeboat station at the end of Harbour Road. Some of you came to last year's event, so please note that we are not using the car park this time, because the council is resurfacing it. If you're driving, there's plenty of space on the road beside the football field, about five minutes' walk away.

Registration opens at 9.15, so that you have time to sign in, collect your gloves and bags and meet your team leader. The leaflet says we begin at 9.30, but that was a printing error. We actually get going at 9.45, once everyone's been given their instructions, and we aim to finish by about 12.30.

Now, a word about what to wear. The forecast looks good, but it can be breezy on the beach, so bring a windproof jacket. Please wear sturdy boots. I know some people like to turn up in sandals or trainers on a day like this, but there's always broken glass and sharp metal along the tideline, and we can't allow anyone on the beach without proper footwear. Wellingtons are fine too, of course. We provide gloves, bags and litter pickers, but do bring sun cream, a hat and your own water bottle, so we don't have to hand out plastic cups.

A reminder for anyone bringing children or teenagers. Everybody under 16 needs to be with an adult at all times, and they must hand in a permission form, signed by a parent or guardian, when they register. You can download the form from our website, and I've also got a few spare copies here on the table.

When we're finished, there'll be something to warm you up. Last year we offered sandwiches, but this year the Bay Café has kindly offered to make a big pot of soup, with bread, and it's free for every volunteer. That will be served in the community hall from 1 o'clock.

Now let me explain who will be doing what. We'll split into five teams, each looking after a different part of the beach, and each with a different job. I'll go through them in the order that you'll see them as you walk down from the lifeboat station.

First, the slipway. The team there has what's probably the most demanding job, because the tide leaves a lot of old fishing nets and rope tangled around the stones. Those can be heavy and they're hard to pull free, so the slipway team will be cutting nets and rope into manageable lengths and carrying them to the skip. If you're strong and don't mind getting a bit muddy, that's the team for you.

Next is the dunes path. This team's job is simpler. They'll walk the length of the path with litter pickers and put everything into the black bags: wrappers, bottles, bits of plastic. The only rule is to stay on the path, because the dune grass is easily damaged, and it's what holds the sand together.

Then we come to Rocky Point. This is where the most interesting rubbish ends up, because the currents trap things between the rocks. We take part in a national survey, so the team at Rocky Point won't just pick things up. They'll count every item and record it on a survey sheet: so many bottle tops, so many cotton buds, and so on. It takes patience, but the figures really do get used by researchers.

The fourth team is based in the car park, where we've put out the recycling bins. Everything collected on the beach is brought there, and this team sorts it into glass, cans and plastics, so that as much as possible is recycled instead of going to landfill. It's a good job if you'd rather stay on dry ground.

And the last team will be on the pier steps. They won't be collecting anything, in fact. They'll be serving hot drinks and biscuits throughout the morning, and keeping an eye out for anyone who's looking cold or tired. We always ask a few people to do that, because it makes a big difference on a windy day.

We did think about asking a team to repair the signs along the path, but we decided to leave that for another weekend. So, to sum up, please arrive from 9.15, wear proper boots, and do pick the team that suits you. You can sign up for a team on the clipboard by the door as you leave today. Thank you very much, and I look forward to seeing you all on Saturday.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two business students plan a pop-up cafe project for their course.
script: Right, Ravi, shall we go through where we've got to with the pop-up cafe project? Dr Hanley wants our outline by Friday.
Yes, let's. First of all, location. I know you were keen on the library foyer.
I was, because it's so quiet, but then I found out that food and drink aren't allowed in there. So that's out.

Which leaves the student union atrium. I did a headcount last Tuesday, and between 11 and 2 something like 900 people walked through. That's far more than pass the sports hall or the main lecture theatres.
Good. And it isn't free, is it? I remember the union wanting a fee.
Only a small one, 15 pounds for the day. It's not the price that matters, it's the footfall. If people see us on their way past, we'll sell more.
Agreed. Now, the menu. I'd really like to do soup at lunchtime. It's cheap to make and people love it.
I'd love that too, but I checked with the union. Anyone preparing hot food has to hold a food hygiene certificate, and neither of us does. The course takes two days and costs more than we'll make.
Hmm. Well, I suppose we shouldn't risk it. So just hot drinks, then, and cakes.
Yes, tea, coffee and hot chocolate, with cakes that we buy ready-made. Packaged things don't need the certificate.
Fine. What about money? By my calculation we need about 160 pounds for stock, cups and the union fee. My uncle said he'd lend it to us.

That's kind, but I'd rather not mix family into the project. Dr Hanley mentioned the department's enterprise fund. It gives up to 200 pounds to student projects, and you just fill in a short application. If we get that, we won't need to use our savings or borrow anything.
That would be much better. I'll write the application tonight.
Brilliant. Now, prices. I was thinking we could charge 2 pounds 80 for a coffee, same as the campus café.
We'd never compete if we're exactly the same. And I had another idea: pay what you like. People put in whatever they think is fair.

It's an interesting idea, but we wouldn't be able to work out our profit margins, and that's what the report is about. I think we should go just under the campus café, say 2 pounds 50 for a coffee. Students will notice the difference.
My biggest worry now is the lunchtime rush. If we've only got one machine, each coffee takes a minute or more, and with 900 people passing, there could be a long queue. People might just walk away.
Then let's plan for that. What about the opening hours? We said 10 until 4, didn't we?
I checked, and the union closes the atrium at 4 for cleaning. We need time to pack up, so we'd better finish at 3.30.
So 10 till 3.30. And staff? I've asked four friends who've said yes.
I've got two more who can help, so with them, that makes 6 helpers in all, not counting us.
That should be plenty. Now, equipment. I've borrowed a toaster from my flatmate, but we won't need it now.
No. The catering department has a big urn that we can borrow to keep the water hot. I asked yesterday, and they said yes as long as we return it clean.
I've been to the bakery on Mill Street. They'll sell us 60 slices at a discount, and they'll deliver them on the morning.
Excellent. Did you decide how we'll gather feedback from customers? Dr Hanley wants something more than numbers.
I thought of a questionnaire, but nobody fills those in. What about filming short comments from customers? We could include a short video in our presentation.
Yes, I like that. It'll make the presentation much more lively than a page of graphs. We'll need to ask permission, though.
Of course. I'll draw up a consent form. Right, shall I type up the outline and send it to you tonight?
Please. And I'll send the funding application to Dr Hanley first thing tomorrow.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer explains how coral reefs form and why they are in danger.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about coral reefs: how they form, why they matter, and why scientists are so worried about their future.

Let me begin with a surprise. Many people think that corals are plants, or even rocks. They are neither. A coral reef is built by tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp is only a few millimetres across, and it is a close relative of the jellyfish. It has a soft body with a ring of tentacles, which it uses to catch plankton drifting past in the water.

What makes polyps remarkable is that they build themselves a hard protective cup. They take calcium out of the seawater and use it to make limestone. When the polyp dies, the cup stays behind, and a new polyp settles on top of it and builds its own. Over thousands of years, those layers add up to a reef. Some branching corals can grow 10 centimetres in a year, though most grow much more slowly.

But polyps cannot do all this on their own. Living inside their tissues are microscopic algae. The algae use sunlight to make sugars, and they pass up to 90 per cent of that food on to the polyp. In return, the polyp provides shelter and the chemicals the algae need. It is also the algae that give corals their wonderful colours.

Because of this partnership, reefs have very particular needs. They need light, so they grow in clear, shallow water, usually no deeper than 50 metres. Some corals do live deeper than that, but they are not reef-builders. Divers often tell me that the most colourful corals are at about 10 metres, and that is true, but the reef itself can grow much deeper. Reefs also need warm water, generally between 23 and 29 degrees.

Now, reefs come in three main shapes. Fringing reefs grow close to the shore, almost like a border along the coast. Barrier reefs lie further out, and are separated from the land by a deep channel or lagoon. The most famous example is off the coast of Australia. Finally, there are atolls, which are rings of coral surrounding a lagoon. Charles Darwin suggested that atolls begin as fringing reefs around a volcanic island, and that the reef keeps growing upwards as the island slowly sinks.

Why should we care? Well, reefs cover less than 1 per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines by absorbing the force of storm waves, and they support fishing and tourism for millions of people.

So what is going wrong? The most widespread threat is rising sea temperature. If the water stays just 1 or 2 degrees warmer than usual for several weeks, the polyps become stressed and expel their algae. Without the algae, the coral loses its colour and turns white. That is what we call bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving, and if the heat continues, it dies. In recent decades we have seen mass bleaching events affect reefs across the tropics.

There are other problems, which tend to be more local. Fishing with explosives is shocking, and it makes the news, but it happens only in a few regions. Tourist boats dropping anchors damage reefs too. Another serious problem is pollution from farms. When fertiliser washes into the sea, it feeds algae in the water, which block the light. It also seems to feed the larvae of the crown-of-thorns starfish. This starfish eats living polyps, and outbreaks of it have destroyed huge areas of reef. Many scientists now believe that the outbreaks are linked to that run-off from farmland, although the evidence is still being collected.

What can be done? Governments can create marine protected areas, where fishing and anchoring are restricted. Local communities can reduce pollution by managing farm run-off. And scientists have developed coral nurseries. They grow small fragments of healthy coral on underwater frames, then plant them on damaged reefs. These projects are encouraging, and they bring hope to the communities that depend on reefs.

However, I do not want to overstate this. Nurseries can only help a damaged reef recover if the water temperature stops rising. If global warming continues at its present rate, new coral will simply bleach again. So the conclusion is that restoration is worth doing, but only alongside serious action to limit warming.
Next week, we'll look at the deep-sea ecosystems that have recently been discovered, and ask whether they face the same threats. Thank you.

passages.title: Kingsmere Sports Club: summer courses for children
paras: Our summer courses run from Monday 21 July to Friday 22 August at the club on Fennimore Road. Each course lasts one week, from Monday to Friday, and is limited to 16 children, so early booking is advised. Booking opens on 2 June for club members and on 9 June for everyone else. All courses are led by qualified instructors, and every child receives a free club T-shirt on the first day.

A  Little Splashers (ages 5-7). Held in the shallow pool from 9.00 to 10.30 am, this course introduces young children to the water in small groups. Parents may watch from the poolside. The fee is 45 pounds.

B  Junior Tennis (ages 8-12). Children learn the basic strokes in two-hour sessions from 10.00 am to 12.00 noon. Rackets and balls are provided. On Friday afternoon, parents are invited to a short match, and prizes are given for effort as well as skill. The fee is 60 pounds.

C  Climbing Wall Adventure (ages 9-14). Sessions run from 1.00 to 3.30 pm. No experience is necessary, as the instructors teach everything from tying knots to safe climbing. Helmets and harnesses are supplied, but all children must wear closed shoes with flat soles, and sandals are not allowed. The fee is 75 pounds.

D  Multi-Sports Camp (ages 6-11). This is our busiest course, running all day from 9.00 am to 3.00 pm. Children try a different sport each day, from badminton to archery. Lunch is not provided, so children should bring a packed lunch and a water bottle. The fee is 110 pounds.

E  Young Coaches (ages 13-15). This course is for teenagers who want to help to run sessions for younger children. It meets from 9.30 am to 12.30 pm. At the end of the week, every participant receives a certificate. Applicants must be members of the club and will be asked to attend a short interview. The fee is 40 pounds.

Brothers and sisters booking together receive a 10 per cent discount on the second course. Payment in full secures your child's place. Refunds are given only if you cancel at least 14 days before the course begins; after that, we can offer a place on another course only if one is free. Booking forms are available at reception or on the club website.

passages.title: Charlton Road: gas main replacement and diversions
paras: Beckfield Gas Networks will be replacing the main gas pipe beneath Charlton Road. Work begins on Monday 8 September and is expected to last about six weeks. We apologise for any inconvenience and have set out below what residents and traders should expect.

Road closure. Charlton Road will be closed to through traffic between the Mill Lane junction and the railway bridge. The rest of the road will stay open. Drivers will be directed along Ashgrove Avenue and Station Road, and the route will be marked by yellow signs. Please allow an extra ten minutes for journeys at busy times.
Buses. Route 14 will not stop at Charlton Parade while the work is in progress. A temporary stop will be provided on Station Road, outside the post office. Timetables will not change.

Working hours. Work will take place from 8.00 am to 6.00 pm, Monday to Friday. Occasionally, work may be needed on Saturday mornings. There will be no work on Sundays or public holidays. Some noise is unavoidable, and we ask for your patience.

Residents and shops. Residents of Charlton Road must move their vehicles from the roadside by 7.00 pm on Sunday 7 September. All the shops on Charlton Parade will remain open, and pedestrians can use the pavements throughout. Delivery lorries should use the service lane behind the shops, which can be reached from Mill Lane. If you have any questions, please telephone our free information line on 0800 555 0142.

passages.title: Handling stock: a guide for new shop assistants at Fairweather Home and Garden
paras: Handling stock correctly keeps our shelves full, our customers happy and our staff safe. Please read this guide carefully before your first shift on the shop floor.

Deliveries. Our main deliveries arrive on Tuesdays and Fridays before the shop opens. Never sign for a delivery until you have checked the contents of each box against the delivery note. If you find that anything is missing or damaged, tell the driver before he leaves and write a note on the delivery note itself. Damaged items must be put in a red crate in the stockroom, and the supervisor will decide what to do with them. Never put a damaged item back on the shelf.

Storage and lifting. Heavy items, such as bags of compost and paving slabs, are kept on the bottom shelves of the stockroom, and lighter ones go above. Any item weighing more than 15 kg must be moved on a trolley. When you lift anything, bend your knees and keep your back straight. If you are not sure that you can lift something safely, ask a colleague to help. Ladders may be used only by staff who have completed the training, and only when another person is holding the bottom.

Filling shelves. The best time to refill shelves is early in the morning or during quiet periods in the afternoon. Old price labels must be removed before new ones are put on, because a double label can confuse the till. Always follow the rule of stock rotation: put new items behind older ones so that the older goods are sold first. This is important for products such as seeds, paint and fertiliser, which have a use-by date.

Customers come first. If a customer asks you a question while you are filling shelves, stop what you are doing and help them. You can finish the shelf afterwards. If you cannot answer the question, take the customer to a colleague who can, rather than telling them where to go. Please keep aisles clear of boxes and trolleys at all times, so that wheelchairs and pushchairs can pass.
Stock counts. Every month, on the last Sunday, we count all the stock in the shop. You will be told in advance if you are needed, and you will be paid at an overtime rate.

passages.title: Data protection: rules for office staff
paras: Our customers trust us with their personal information, and the law requires us to look after it carefully. Everybody who works in our offices must follow these rules.

Computers and passwords. Lock your screen whenever you leave your desk, even for a minute. Passwords must be changed every 90 days. They must never be shared with anyone, including your manager or the IT department. Do not write them on paper.

Paper files. Customer files must be locked in a cabinet at the end of each day, and your desk should be clear when you leave. Documents containing personal details must not be left on printers or photocopiers. We keep customer files for six years after an account is closed, and they are then shredded.

Email. Always check the address before you send a message containing personal data. If you are writing to a group of customers, use blind copy so that the addresses of other customers are not visible. Do not send customer details to a private email account.
Memory sticks and devices. Personal data may be stored on a portable memory stick only if the stick is encrypted. Staff must not use their own devices to store customer details.

Breaches. If you think that personal data has been lost, stolen or sent to the wrong person, you must tell the Data Protection Officer within 24 hours. You must do this even if you are not certain that a breach has taken place. It is much better to report a problem that turns out to be nothing than to hide a real one.
Training. All new employees must complete the data protection course within their first month. The course is repeated every year, and managers will check that everyone has completed it.

passages.title: The public library: a short history
paras: A  Long before anyone imagined a library open to everyone, books were treasures. Each copy was written out by hand, which took months, so only monasteries, universities and rich families could afford a collection. Even after printing made books cheaper in the fifteenth century, most ordinary people could not buy them. From the eighteenth century, subscription libraries appeared in many British towns: members paid a yearly fee and in return could borrow from a shared stock of books. Commercial lending libraries, which charged a small sum for each volume, served some people who could not afford a subscription, yet the poorest readers were still shut out.

B  The change came in the nineteenth century, when factories drew families into fast-growing cities. Reformers worried about how workers spent their free time. They argued that a free reading room would offer a respectable alternative to the tavern, and that a literate population would be more productive and better behaved. Others were less enthusiastic, and some ratepayers objected to paying for books they would never read themselves. Even so, in 1850 Parliament passed a law allowing town councils to raise a small local tax to set up libraries. The first law, however, allowed the money to be spent only on buildings and staff, not on books, so early libraries depended on gifts from local residents to fill their shelves.

C  Wealthy benefactors helped to fill the gap. The most famous was the steel manufacturer Andrew Carnegie, who paid for about 2,500 libraries in towns across the English-speaking world. His gifts came with strings attached: the community had to provide the land and promise to pay for the running costs every year. This meant that a town could not simply accept a grand building and then let it decay. Many places that had been reluctant to tax themselves for a library now found it hard to refuse a free building, and so the movement spread quickly.

D  Inside, however, early public libraries were run strictly. Books were kept in closed stacks, and readers had to consult a printed catalogue, fill in a request slip and wait while an assistant fetched the volume. Borrowers needed a guarantor, usually a local householder, who would vouch for them. Librarians feared theft and damage, and some libraries even used indicator boards that showed which books were out on loan. Only towards the end of the century did a few pioneering librarians introduce open access, which allowed readers to walk among the shelves and choose for themselves. Many colleagues predicted chaos and heavy losses. In practice, borrowing rose sharply and the losses were small.

E  The twentieth century widened the audience. Special children's rooms opened, with low shelves and story hours, and many adults first entered a library as parents. Branch libraries spread through the suburbs, so that nobody lived far from one, and mobile libraries, converted from buses and vans, carried books to villages and farms. Libraries began to lend records and later films as well as books, and librarianship grew into a profession with its own training and qualifications.

F  Yet the late twentieth century brought new pressures. As home computers and then the internet arrived, some commentators predicted that libraries would become obsolete: why visit a building when information is available on a screen? At the same time, councils faced tighter budgets, and many closed branches or reduced their opening hours. In some places, the number of borrowers did fall.

G  Supporters replied that the critics had misunderstood what libraries are for. Free internet access matters most to people who cannot afford a computer at home. Libraries now offer help with job applications, classes for new arrivals learning the language, homework clubs and quiet places to study. Some lend tools, seeds and even musical instruments. Electronic books and audio can be borrowed through a phone app, which has brought back readers who had not visited for years.

H  The history of the public library is therefore a story of repeated reinvention. It began as a charity-funded experiment, grew into a municipal service and now acts as a community hub. Whether it can survive depends less on technology than on a simple political question: whether societies are still willing to pay for a space that belongs to everyone.
